lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you met trade around the world. What is an export? (Something a country sells to another.) People move between places too. Today: migration.

Migration means moving to live somewhere else. It can be inside one country, such as from a village to a city, or from one country to another. People have always moved: the Anglo-Saxons and Vikings were migrants too.

Push factors make people want to leave a place: no jobs, poor schools or hospitals, droughts, floods or war. Pull factors draw them to a new place: jobs, better pay, safety, family and friends, schools and hospitals.
Most people choose to move. Some are forced to flee danger such as war or disasters. People who must flee their country for safety are called refugees, and many countries have agreed to protect them.
Moving is not easy. Barriers include the cost of travel, long distances, learning a new language and missing family. Each country also makes rules about who may come to live there.

A place's population changes in two ways: natural change (births take away deaths) and migration (people moving in take away people moving out). Worked example: 300 − 200 = 100 more from births; 150 − 50 = 100 more from moving; 100 + 100 = 200 in all.
Migration changes both places. Newcomers bring skills, food, music and languages, and fill jobs. Places people leave may have fewer young workers, but families often receive money sent home.
Try it in the world: put up two signs in your village: reasons to come (pull) and reasons people left (push). Count who moves in and out of your village in a week. Next: cities.

exercises.hint: It is about where people live.
exercises.explain: Moving to live in a new place, in the same country or another one.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: push factor or pull factor?
exercises.hint: Push makes you leave; pull draws you in.
exercises.explain: Push: no jobs at home, a long drought. Pull: better pay, family already there.

exercises.prompt: Refugees are people forced to flee their country for safety.
exercises.hint: Think of the difference between choosing to move and having to.
exercises.explain: True: refugees must flee danger, and many countries have agreed to protect them.

exercises.hint: A pull factor draws people to a place.
exercises.explain: Good schools and hospitals draw people in.

exercises.prompt: A family moves from a village to a city in the same country. What is this?
exercises.hint: Migration can be inside a country or between countries.
exercises.explain: It is migration inside one country, often from the countryside to a city.

exercises.prompt: In one year 420 people moved to a town and 170 moved away. By how many did moving change the population?
exercises.hint: Take the people who left from the people who came.

exercises.prompt: A town had 500 births and 350 deaths in a year. What was its natural change?
exercises.hint: Natural change is births take away deaths.

exercises.prompt: Which is a barrier to migration?
exercises.explain: The cost of travel can stop people moving.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Two are reasons; one is a person; one gets in the way.
exercises.explain: Push: a reason to leave. Pull: a reason to come. Refugee: forced to flee. Barrier: makes moving hard.

exercises.prompt: Most migrants are forced to move.
exercises.hint: Look back at the card on choosing and fleeing.
exercises.explain: False: most people choose to move, for work, family or study; some are forced to flee.

exercises.prompt: A town started the year with 5,000 people. It had 120 births and 80 deaths; 60 people moved in and 140 moved out. How many people at the end of the year?
exercises.hint: Work out the change first; it may be less than 0.

exercises.prompt: A family moves from a farm to a city for work. Which pair is right?
exercises.hint: Push is at the old home; pull is at the new one.
choices: push: few jobs; pull: work in the city
push: work in the city; pull: few jobs
exercises.explain: The push is few jobs on the farm; the pull is work in the city.

exercises.prompt: How can migration help the place people leave?
exercises.hint: Think of families who stay behind.
exercises.explain: Many migrants send money home, which helps their families and towns.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: natural change, or migration?
exercises.hint: Natural change is about births and deaths.
exercises.explain: Natural change: births and deaths. Migration: people moving in or out, like a family arriving from abroad.

exercises.prompt: A town's population can fall even if it has more births than deaths.
exercises.explain: True: if many more people move out than move in, the population can still fall.
